title: Entanglement
kicker: Two qubits with one shared state that neither has on its own.
summary: Some two-qubit states cannot be split into a state for each qubit. In these entangled states the measurement results are correlated more strongly than any pre-arranged classical plan allows. Entanglement is a resource: teleportation, superdense coding and many algorithms consume it.

blocks.heading: A state for the pair, not for each qubit
blocks.body:
Two independent qubits in states a|0⟩ + b|1⟩ and c|0⟩ + d|1⟩ together have the *product state* ac|00⟩ + ad|01⟩ + bc|10⟩ + bd|11⟩.

Now take (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. To write it as a product you would need ad = 0 and bc = 0, while ac and bd are both non-zero. That is impossible, so this state cannot be described qubit by qubit. It is *entangled*.

blocks.title: Making a Bell state
blocks.caption: Hadamard on qubit 0, then CNOT from qubit 0 to qubit 1, gives (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. Only 00 and 11 are ever measured.

ops.note: CNOT copies qubit 0's value into qubit 1 in each branch: (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2.

blocks.heading: Perfect correlation, random results
blocks.body:
Measure either qubit of (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 and you get 0 or 1 with probability ½ each. Measure the other one afterwards and it always matches.

The four *Bell states* are the standard basis of maximally entangled two-qubit states. (A gate applied to just one qubit of a Bell state gives another maximally entangled state, so there are infinitely many.) Starting the same circuit from |01⟩, |10⟩ or |11⟩ produces the other three.

blocks.title: Another Bell state
blocks.caption: Start from |01⟩ and run the same circuit: (|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2. Now the two results always disagree.

blocks.title: One qubit alone looks like noise
blocks.caption: Looking only at qubit 1 of the Bell state, the outcomes are 50/50, whatever is done to qubit 0. This is why entanglement cannot send a message.

ops.note: Even a gate on qubit 0 leaves qubit 1's own statistics unchanged.

blocks.myth: Measuring one entangled qubit sends a signal to the other, faster than light.
blocks.truth: The other side's results are 50/50 whatever the first side does. The correlation only appears when the two lists of results are compared, which needs ordinary communication. No information travels through entanglement alone (the no-signalling principle).

blocks.myth: Entanglement is just shared hidden instructions, like two sealed envelopes.
blocks.truth: Bell's theorem shows that no such local plan can reproduce all the correlations entangled qubits give when measured in different bases. Experiments have confirmed the quantum predictions.

blocks.question: In the state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 you measure qubit 0 and get 1. What will qubit 1 give, and with what probability?
blocks.hint: Which terms of the state are left once qubit 0 is known to be 1?
blocks.answer: Only |11⟩ is consistent with qubit 0 being 1, so the state becomes |11⟩ and qubit 1 gives 1 with probability 1.

sources.title: M. A. Nielsen and I. L. Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information (10th anniversary ed., Cambridge University Press, 2010), ch. 1–2
J. S. Bell, "On the Einstein Podolsky Rosen paradox", Physics 1, 195 (1964)
